source.title: Compute Better Spent: Replacing Dense Layers with Structured Matrices
source.authors: Shi-Kai Qiu; Andres Potapczynski; Marc Finzi; Micah Goldblum; Andrew Gordon Wilson

record.tranche_reason: The study measures how scaling with compute changes across structured-layer choices and reports that scaling exponents depend on structure; it also distinguishes training-error power laws from test-error curves that are not well described by a power law.
record.gate_note: The study reports comparative scaling results for image-model training error, image-model test error, ImageNet validation error, and GPT-2 validation loss. Some exact curve values and fitted exponents appear only in figures and are not recoverable from the supplied text. Statements about prior work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: Its own CIFAR experiments fit power laws of training error against compute, which bears on V5. They also show the fitted exponent changes with layer structure, which bears on V7. The paper argues exponents are not set by the task alone. ImageNet and GPT-2 results are only efficiency comparisons of the authors' method against dense layers, with no power-law fit.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add three points. The authors stress that structure-aware (µP-based) learning rates are essential. They find that structures whose parameter count matches their FLOPs scale best. They add that the GPT-2 gain comes mainly from cheaper LM-head compute and may diminish at larger scale.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares width-scaled networks with alternative structured matrix parameterizations and measures error or validation loss against compute. It does not reproduce the original language-model parameter/token/compute sweeps or compute-optimal allocation method.
record.method_sensitivity: Scaling results vary by matrix structure and by structured-layer settings such as BTT rank and Monarch block count. The GPT-2 comparison changes substantially depending on whether language-modeling-head compute is included. Training-error and test-error curves also differ.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched compute, swapping dense layers for structured matrices changes the scaling exponent. The authors contrast this with Kaplan's view that architecture details matter little and with task-determined exponent theories.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layer parameterization (structure of linear layers) at fixed compute can change compute-scaling exponents, not just offsets.

fits_no_version.finding: The GPT-2 BTT advantage appears when total compute is counted and vanishes for non-embedding compute.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute-accounting conventions (including or excluding the LM head) determine apparent efficiency gains in LM scaling comparisons.

record.problems: The authors state that evaluation is primarily on relatively small-scale models and datasets; training iterations are fixed rather than compute-optimised; comparisons use FLOPs rather than runtime; and findings may be dataset-dependent. Many fitted exponents and curve values are only shown in figures, not numerically stated in the supplied text.

untested.parts: No fit of held-out LM loss against parameters, tokens or compute; GPT-2 has only 3 dense and 4 BTT points without a fit.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
Iterations are fixed; compute-optimal allocation is explicitly left to future work.
Depth, width and shape at fixed parameter count are not varied; depth is held constant.
Video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested; ImageNet and GPT-2 have no fits.
Fitting method, training schedule and data choices are not varied. Parameter-counting effects appear only qualitatively (GPT-2 LM head).

missing.what: Without structure-aware learning rates, structured models' performance saturates as they scale (curve bends), so the scaling curve depends on the learning-rate parameterization.
Gaps between BTT ranks close as width grows, so curves for different configurations converge at scale.
Below about 1e7 FLOPs, runtime barely changes with FLOPs, obscuring scaling laws measured in runtime.

record.verdict_notes: Scaling is in per-forward compute with fixed iterations, and models are near but not at convergence. The measure is training error on an augmented dataset, not held-out pretraining loss. Exponent values and standard errors appear only in figures. ImageNet and GPT-2 rows compare the authors' method with dense layers and carry no fits, so they are unlinked.

versions.untested_parts: It does not test held-out pretraining loss scaling against parameter count, tokens, or compute for language models when the other quantities are not bottlenecks.
It does not fit scaling laws on small runs and test predictions on runs orders of magnitude larger.
The study holds training iterations fixed and explicitly leaves compute-optimal allocation between model compute and training steps to future work.
It does not isolate depth, width, or other architecture details at a fixed parameter count.

Image-classification scaling is tested, and GPT-2 validation loss is compared across compute, but the paper does not establish the same power-law form across modalities and regimes generally. Video, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested.
It does not test downstream-task performance as a function of pretraining loss or scale.

The study shows dependence on matrix structure and a difference between training-error and test-error curves. It does not test sensitivity to parameter-counting conventions or fitting methods, nor whether published compute-optimal splits disagree.

rows.subject: CIFAR-10 MLP, BTT rank sweep
rows.operation_detail: Varied BTT rank while comparing training error at matched FLOPs.

rows.check: The value is garbled. The text says higher-rank BTTs scale better than dense, but lower-rank BTTs have lower error per FLOP. This is an efficiency offset between configurations of the study's own method, with no exponent comparison.

source_check.notes: These are fixed-iteration width sweeps using structure-aware learning rates, not compute-optimal allocation experiments. Individual fitted exponents are not numerically recoverable from the supplied text; FLOPs are used as a stand-in for MACs.
